terms.def: A way energy can be held. There are eight types: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: Energy stored in a moving object; calculated using Ek = ½mv², where m is mass (kg) and v is speed (m/s); measured in joules (J)
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: Energy stored in an object due to its height above a reference point; calculated using Ep = mgh, where g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth; measured in joules (J)
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed object; calculated using Ee = ½ke², where k is the spring constant (N/m) and e is the extension (m); measured in joules (J)
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: Energy transferred by work done by forces — e.g. pushing, pulling, kicking

terms.term: Electrical transfer (work done when a current flows)
terms.def: Energy transferred by work done when a current flows in a circuit
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: Energy transferred from a hotter object to a cooler one by conduction or convection; always flows from higher to lower temperature. Radiation is a separate pathway.
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: Energy transferred by electromagnetic waves, such as light and infrared
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can be transferred usefully, stored or dissipated; total energy in a closed system is always constant
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: A system in which no energy is transferred to or from the surroundings — the total energy remains constant
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: The spreading of energy into the thermal store of the surroundings, making it less useful — most real energy transfers dissipate some energy
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: Energy transferred to a store that is not useful for the intended purpose of the device — most commonly dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: A flow diagram where the width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy — the input arrow splits into useful output and wasted energy arrows
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: The ratio of useful output energy (or power) to total input energy (or power); efficiency = useful output ÷ total input; always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%)
terms.lessonName: Energy stores and transfers — what energy actually is

terms.def: The energy an object has due to its motion; Ek = ½mv², where m is mass (kg) and v is speed (m/s); measured in joules (J)
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: The SI unit of energy and work — 1 J = 1 N m = the energy transferred when a force of 1 N moves an object 1 m in the direction of the force
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: Energy stored in an object due to its height above a reference point; Ep = mgh, where m is mass (kg), g is gravitational field strength (N/kg), and h is height (m); measured in joules (J)
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: The gravitational force acting per unit mass; about 9.8 N/kg on Earth's surface — always use the value given in the question; unit: N/kg
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between stores or dissipated; the total energy in a closed system remains constant
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: The movement of energy from one store to another (e.g. gravitational potential → kinetic as an object falls), or the spreading of energy as dissipation
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: Energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object; Ee = ½ke², where k is the spring constant (N/m) and e is the extension (m); measured in joules (J)
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: A measure of the stiffness of a spring; k = F ÷ e, where F is the force (N) and e is the extension (m); unit: N/m — higher k means a stiffer spring
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: The increase in length of a spring beyond its natural (unstretched) length; e = stretched length − natural length; measured in metres (m)
terms.lessonName: Kinetic and potential energy — the equations

terms.def: Energy spread out into the surroundings, usually as thermal energy, where it is difficult to use again
terms.lessonName: Conservation of energy and energy dissipation

terms.def: Energy transferred to the intended output store
terms.lessonName: Conservation of energy and energy dissipation

terms.def: Using oil or similar material between surfaces to reduce friction, so less energy is dissipated by heating
terms.lessonName: Conservation of energy and energy dissipation

terms.def: A force between surfaces. When an object moves against friction, work is done and energy is transferred to the thermal store
terms.lessonName: Conservation of energy and energy dissipation

terms.def: A material or design that slows the transfer of thermal energy to the surroundings
terms.lessonName: Conservation of energy and energy dissipation

terms.def: The higher the thermal conductivity, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction
terms.lessonName: Conservation of energy and energy dissipation

terms.def: Shaping an object to reduce air resistance, so less energy is dissipated
terms.lessonName: Conservation of energy and energy dissipation

terms.def: Energy transferred to the intended output store — the energy that does the job we want
All energy supplied to a device, including both useful and wasted portions
efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer (or useful power output ÷ total power input)
Old-style filament light bulb — wastes most of its input energy by heating
Light Emitting Diode — more efficient than a filament bulb at transferring energy usefully as light
The rate of energy transfer; P = E/t; unit: watts (W)

terms.def: The unit of power; 1 W = 1 joule per second (1 J/s)
terms.lessonName: Power — how fast energy is transferred

terms.def: How quickly something happens — here, how many joules transferred per second
terms.lessonName: Power — how fast energy is transferred

terms.def: Power equals energy divided by time; rearranges to E = Pt and t = E/P
terms.lessonName: Power — how fast energy is transferred

terms.def: 1000 watts — unit used for powerful appliances and small generators

terms.def: 1,000,000 watts — unit used for power stations and large industrial outputs
terms.lessonName: Power — how fast energy is transferred

terms.def: 1,000,000,000 watts — unit used for national power output and very large power stations

terms.def: W = Fs; energy transferred when a force moves an object, where s is the distance moved along the line of action of the force; unit: joule (J)
terms.lessonName: Power — how fast energy is transferred

terms.def: 1 N m = 1 J; the work done when a force of 1 N causes a displacement of 1 m
terms.lessonName: Power — how fast energy is transferred

terms.def: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C; unit: J/kg°C

terms.lessonName: Heating and cooling — specific heat capacity

terms.lessonName: Heating and cooling — specific heat capacity

terms.def: An instrument that directly measures electrical energy in joules

terms.def: The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system
terms.lessonName: Heating and cooling — specific heat capacity

terms.def: How hot or cold something is, measured in °C. It is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles
terms.lessonName: Heating and cooling — specific heat capacity

terms.def: The network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to consumers across the UK

terms.def: A transformer that increases the potential difference
terms.lessonName: Energy resources and the National Grid

terms.def: A transformer that decreases the potential difference
terms.lessonName: Energy resources and the National Grid

terms.def: An energy resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used — wind, solar, hydro, the tides, water waves, geothermal, bio-fuel
terms.lessonName: Energy resources and the National Grid

terms.def: Energy resource that will run out — fossil fuels (coal, gas, oil) and nuclear (uranium)
terms.lessonName: Energy resources and the National Grid

terms.def: Not always available — solar cells do not work at night, and wind turbines only work when the wind blows

terms.def: What flows round a circuit. It is carried by tiny particles in the wire. Measured in coulombs (C).
The amount of charge that passes a point, in coulombs (C).
A flow of charge. Its size is the rate of flow: how much charge passes a point each second. Measured in amperes (A).
The unit of charge.
The unit of current. 1 ampere is 1 coulomb of charge passing each second.
A complete loop. Charge flows round it only if it also includes a source of potential difference, such as a cell.
A part that opens or closes a gap in a circuit, to stop or start the current.
A meter that measures current. It goes in the loop, in line with the component.
The push that makes charge flow through a component. Measured in volts (V). Also called voltage.
The unit of potential difference. 1 volt is 1 joule per coulomb.
Another name for potential difference.
A component that limits the current in a circuit.
A meter that measures potential difference. It is connected across a component.
How much a component opposes the current through it. Measured in ohms (Ω).
The unit of resistance. 1 ohm is 1 volt per ampere.
Any part of a circuit, such as a lamp, a resistor or a diode.
Connected one after another in the same loop, so the same current flows through each.
Connected side by side, across the same two points.
The temperature stays the same throughout the measurements.
A graph of current (up the side) against potential difference (along the bottom) for a component.
When one quantity doubles, the other doubles too. The graph is a straight line through the origin.
A component whose resistance stays constant at constant temperature. Its I-V graph is a straight line through the origin.
A bulb with a thin metal wire (the filament) that glows when hot. Its resistance increases as it gets hotter.
A component that lets current flow in one direction only. It has a very high resistance in the reverse direction.
A resistor whose resistance you can change, often with a slider. Used to change the current in a circuit.
Gives a straight-line graph.
Gives a graph that is not a straight line, such as the curve of a filament lamp or the graph of a diode.
The energy passed on as charge flows through a component, in joules (J).
In a circuit, a bulb is called a lamp.
When charge flows through a component, work is done: energy is transferred from the charge to the component.
Components connected in a single loop with no branches; current has only one path
Sum of individual resistances: Rtotal = R1 + R2 +...
Components in separate branches between the same two points; the potential difference across each component is the same
Mains circuits wired so every appliance gets full supply potential difference and can be switched independently
A single resistance value that has the same effect on the circuit as a combination of resistors
The standard drawing for a component in a circuit diagram.
A drawing of a circuit made from circuit symbols joined by straight lines for the wires.
A diode that gives out light when a current flows through it.
Something that pushes charge round a circuit. Symbol: a long thin line next to a short thick one.
Two or more cells joined together.
A component whose resistance decreases as its temperature increases.
A part that detects a change around it, such as a thermistor (temperature) or an LDR (light).
A control that keeps a room or an oven at a set temperature. It can use a thermistor to sense the temperature.
A component whose resistance decreases as the light intensity on it increases.
How bright the light is.
The other is the light-dependent resistor ( LDR), which reacts to light.
A potential difference that stays in one direction, so current flows one way only. Produced by batteries and cells.
terms.lessonName: Mains electricity — AC, DC and household circuits

terms.def: A potential difference that keeps reversing direction, so current reverses too. The UK mains is about 230 V, 50 Hz.
terms.lessonName: Mains electricity — AC, DC and household circuits

terms.def: The number of complete ac cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz). UK mains = 50 Hz.
terms.lessonName: Mains electricity — AC, DC and household circuits

terms.def: The brown wire in three-core cable; carries the 230 V ac supply potential difference and is the most dangerous wire.
terms.lessonName: Mains electricity — AC, DC and household circuits

terms.def: The blue wire; completes the circuit and returns current to the supply at approximately 0 V.
terms.lessonName: Mains electricity — AC, DC and household circuits

terms.def: The green and yellow striped wire; a safety wire that connects the metal casing to earth and stops the appliance becoming live.
terms.lessonName: Mains electricity — AC, DC and household circuits

terms.def: Connecting the metal casing of an appliance to earth via the earth wire, so the appliance cannot become live.
terms.lessonName: Mains electricity — AC, DC and household circuits

terms.def: Energy transferred (J) = charge flow (C) × potential difference (V). Connects the electrical quantities to the concept of work done.

terms.def: A calculation requiring two or more equations applied in sequence.
terms.lessonName: Electrical power and energy — cost of electricity

terms.def: The transfer of electrons between two insulating surfaces when rubbed together, causing one to become positive and the other negative.
The material that loses electrons is left with a positive charge. It is equal in size to the negative charge on the other material.
A material that does not allow charge to flow through it easily; static charge can build up on insulators.
The force pulling objects together; two objects that carry different types of charge attract.
The force pushing objects apart; two objects that carry the same type of charge repel.
A huge spark from a charged storm cloud, to another cloud or to the ground.
A region of space around a charged object where another charge experiences a force.
Lines drawn to represent an electric field; show the direction of force on a positive test charge. Closer lines = stronger field.
Charge jumping through the air when the electric field near a charged object is strong enough.
A regular, repeating arrangement of particles in a solid

terms.def: Virtually cannot be compressed — volume hardly changes under pressure
terms.lessonName: States of matter and the particle model

terms.def: Attractive forces between particles that hold them together
terms.lessonName: States of matter and the particle model

terms.def: Energy stored due to the forces of attraction between particles
terms.lessonName: States of matter and the particle model

terms.def: The temperature at which a substance changes from solid to liquid (same as freezing point)
terms.lessonName: States of matter and the particle model

terms.def: The specific temperature at which a liquid boils throughout its volume
terms.lessonName: States of matter and the particle model

terms.def: A change of state directly from solid to gas without passing through liquid
terms.lessonName: States of matter and the particle model

terms.def: A simplified representation of reality used to explain and predict observations
terms.lessonName: States of matter and the particle model

terms.def: The spreading out of particles from high to low concentration due to random motion
terms.lessonName: States of matter and the particle model

terms.def: Mass per unit volume — how much mass is packed into a given space. Symbol: ρ (rho). Unit: kg/m³
The density equation: density equals mass divided by volume
1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Multiply by 1000 to convert g/cm³ to kg/m³
A displacement can filled to the brim — used to measure the volume of an irregular object by collecting the water it displaces
The volume of liquid pushed aside when an object is submerged — equals the volume of the object
How close together and how regular the particles are. It explains the density of each state
Energy absorbed or released during a change of state — does not cause a temperature change

terms.def: A graph of temperature vs time (or energy) showing flat sections at melting and boiling points
terms.lessonName: Changes of state and latent heat

terms.def: A graph of temperature vs time as a substance cools, with flat sections where it condenses or freezes
terms.lessonName: Changes of state and latent heat

terms.def: Energy per kg needed to melt (or freeze) a substance at constant temperature. Unit: J/kg
terms.lessonName: Changes of state and latent heat

terms.def: Energy per kg needed to boil (or condense) a substance at constant temperature. Unit: J/kg
terms.lessonName: Changes of state and latent heat

terms.def: Energy = mass × specific latent heat. The equation for calculating energy in a change of state
terms.lessonName: Changes of state and latent heat

terms.def: The force per unit area exerted by gas molecules colliding with container walls
A molecule striking the container wall — each collision exerts a tiny force contributing to total pressure
Related to the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules
The gas stays in the same space, for example a sealed rigid container
For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, pressure × volume stays the same; p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
When one quantity doubles, the other halves — their product stays constant
The transfer of energy by a force
Thomson's model: a sphere of diffuse positive charge with electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a pudding

terms.def: A tiny, negatively charged particle in the atom; discovered by Thomson in 1897
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: Rutherford's 1909 experiment: alpha particles fired at thin gold foil; results showed atoms have a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: Atomic model proposed by Rutherford: tiny, dense, positive nucleus at the centre with electrons orbiting in empty space
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: A particle consisting of 2 protons + 2 neutrons; positively charged; used as the 'probe' in Rutherford's experiment
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: The number of protons in the nucleus; determines which element the atom is
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: A neutral particle in the nucleus; relative mass 1, relative charge 0
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons: same atomic number, different mass number
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: An atom that has lost one or more outer electrons, so it has an overall positive charge
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: A fixed amount of energy an electron can have; each level is at a specific distance from the nucleus, and electrons move between levels by absorbing or emitting electromagnetic radiation
terms.lessonName: The nuclear model of the atom

terms.def: Radiation that knocks electrons off atoms, creating ions — alpha is the most ionising of alpha, beta and gamma
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays; measured in becquerels (Bq)
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector, such as a Geiger-Muller tube
A fast electron emitted from the nucleus when a neutron converts to a proton; stopped by thin aluminium
A neutron in the nucleus converts to a proton, emitting a beta particle (electron) — atomic number increases by 1
High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus; no mass or charge; weakly ionising but very penetrating
Waves that travel at the speed of light; gamma rays are the highest energy part of the EM spectrum
Low-level radiation from natural and man-made sources always present in the environment
An equation showing radioactive decay with mass numbers and atomic numbers balanced on both sides
The unit of radiation dose; 1000 millisieverts (mSv) = 1 sievert (Sv)
The time for the number of nuclei of a radioactive isotope in a sample to halve, or for its count rate (or activity) to fall to half
The unit of radioactive activity; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second
A curve where the quantity halves in equal time intervals — the shape of all radioactive decay graphs
A graph of activity vs time showing an exponential curve — used to determine half-life
A radioactive isotope (gamma emitter, short half-life) used to explore internal organs; detected outside the body
Using radiation to control or destroy unwanted tissue, such as a tumour; the radiation comes from a beam or a source inside the body
Exposing an object to nuclear radiation; the object does not become radioactive
The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials; the hazard comes from their decay
Other scientists checking published findings before they are accepted
The splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, usually after it absorbs a neutron; it gives out 2 or 3 neutrons, gamma rays and energy
The two smaller nuclei and the neutrons made in fission; all of them have kinetic energy
A uranium isotope used as fuel in nuclear reactors; it splits after absorbing a neutron
Each fission releases neutrons that cause more fissions; controlled, it runs at a steady rate; uncontrolled, it grows rapidly and causes an explosion
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus; some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation
A quantity with magnitude only, no direction (e.g. speed, mass, distance)

terms.def: A quantity with both magnitude and direction (e.g. velocity, force, displacement)

terms.def: Total distance divided by total time for a journey
terms.lessonName: Forces and motion — speed, velocity, acceleration

terms.def: Slope of a graph — on a d-t graph, gradient equals speed
terms.lessonName: Forces and motion — speed, velocity, acceleration

terms.def: Rate of change of velocity, measured in m/s²; can be positive (speeding up) or negative (slowing down)

terms.def: Negative acceleration — the object is slowing down
terms.lessonName: Forces and motion — speed, velocity, acceleration

terms.def: The five motion quantities: displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time

terms.def: Constant falling speed reached when air resistance exactly balances weight, giving zero resultant force

terms.def: Falling under gravity alone with no air resistance; acceleration = g ≈ 9.8 m/s²

terms.def: A force between objects that are physically touching, such as friction, air resistance, tension or normal contact force
terms.lessonName: Forces and motion — speed, velocity, acceleration

terms.def: A force between objects that are physically separated, such as gravitational, electrostatic or magnetic force

terms.def: The single force that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting on an object combined
The tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion; measured by its mass
Unit of force; 1N accelerates a 1kg mass at 1 m/s²
Mass measured by resistance to acceleration using F = ma; equal to gravitational mass
Two forces that are equal, opposite, same type, and act on two different interacting objects
The gravitational force on an object; W = mg, measured in newtons
A diagram showing all forces acting on a single object as labelled arrows
Total distance from first noticing a hazard to coming to a complete stop; equals thinking distance + braking distance
Distance travelled during the driver's reaction time before brakes are applied; = speed × reaction time
Distance travelled while the brakes are applied and the vehicle decelerates to rest
The time between detecting a hazard and pressing the brake — typically 0.2–0.9 seconds for an alert driver
The force applied by the brakes to decelerate the vehicle; transferred from kinetic energy to thermal energy in the brakes
Reduction in braking effectiveness caused by overheated brakes — a hazard during prolonged or repeated heavy braking
The product of an object's mass and velocity: p = mv; measured in kg m/s; a vector quantity with direction
A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction — e.g. momentum, velocity, force
In a closed system (no external forces), the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after
Force multiplied by time (FΔt) — equal to the change in momentum; measured in N s (equivalent to kg m/s)
The difference between final and initial momentum: Δp = mv − mu; caused by a resultant force acting over time
The amount of matter in an object, measured in kg — constant regardless of location
The equation for weight: weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N/kg)
A region of space around a mass where other masses experience a gravitational force — field strength decreases with distance from the mass
The resultant force directed towards the centre of a circle, keeping an object in circular motion — for orbits, this force is provided by gravity
The time taken for one complete orbit — longer for higher orbits
A change of shape where the object goes back to its first shape and length when the forces are removed
A change of shape where the object does not go back to its first shape when the forces are removed
The point after which extension is no longer directly proportional to force
A straight-line graph through the origin; the two quantities are directly proportional
A curved graph; the two quantities are not directly proportional
The turning effect of a force; M = Fd, measured in newton-metres (Nm)
The fixed point that an object turns about
Total clockwise moment about a pivot equals total anticlockwise moment about that pivot
A bar that turns about a pivot; a small force far from the pivot gives a large force close to it
A wheel with teeth that turns another gear; it transmits the rotational effect of a force
A liquid or a gas

terms.def: The force normal to a surface divided by the area of that surface; p = F/A, measured in pascals (Pa)
terms.lessonName: Pressure in fluids and atmospheric pressure

terms.def: The unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m²
terms.lessonName: Pressure in fluids and atmospheric pressure

terms.def: Pressure due to a column of liquid = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength
terms.lessonName: Pressure in fluids and atmospheric pressure

terms.def: The resultant upward force on an object in a liquid, caused by greater pressure on its bottom surface than its top
terms.lessonName: Pressure in fluids and atmospheric pressure

terms.def: A thin layer of air round the Earth, thin compared with the size of the Earth
terms.lessonName: Pressure in fluids and atmospheric pressure

terms.def: The pressure created by air molecules colliding with a surface; it decreases as height increases
terms.lessonName: Pressure in fluids and atmospheric pressure

terms.def: A wave where oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer — e.g. light, water waves
A wave where oscillation is parallel to the direction of energy transfer — e.g. sound
A region of high pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles are pushed together
A region of low pressure in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread apart
Maximum displacement of a wave from its equilibrium (rest) position; larger amplitude means more energy
Distance between two successive points in phase, e.g. crest to crest; measured in metres
Time for one complete wave cycle; T = 1/f; measured in seconds
v = fλ; wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)
How fast the wave travels through the medium; measured in m/s
Wave bounces off a surface; angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both from the normal
Change in wave speed at a boundary causing a change in direction (frequency unchanged)
Spreading of waves around an obstacle or through a gap; greatest when gap ≈ wavelength
An imaginary line perpendicular to a surface, used as the reference for measuring angles of incidence and reflection
A transverse wave that can travel through a vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m/s; consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields
3 × 10⁸ m/s — the speed of all EM waves in a vacuum
The complete range of EM radiation ordered by frequency (or wavelength), from radio waves to gamma rays
The narrow band of EM spectrum detectable by the human eye; wavelengths ~400–700 nm; red to violet
EM waves just below visible light in frequency; associated with thermal energy; used in remote controls and thermal cameras
EM waves just above visible light in frequency; used in sterilisation; can cause skin cancer
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection; both measured from the normal to the surface
Reflection from a smooth surface where all parallel rays reflect at the same angle, forming a clear image
Reflection from a rough surface where rays scatter in many directions, producing no clear image
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal inside the new medium
Complete reflection of light back into a denser medium when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
The angle of incidence at which the refracted ray travels along the boundary; above this, TIR occurs
A thin glass or plastic fibre that uses total internal reflection to transmit light signals along its length
A convex lens, thicker in the middle, that refracts parallel rays to meet at the focal point
The point where parallel rays converge after passing through a converging lens
Distance from the lens centre to the focal point
An image formed where light rays actually cross; can be projected on a screen; always inverted
An image from which rays appear to diverge; cannot be projected; always upright
A wave that requires a physical medium (particles) to travel — cannot travel through a vacuum
The rate at which sound travels through a medium; ~340 m/s in air at room temperature; faster in denser media
The perceived highness or lowness of a sound; determined by frequency — higher frequency = higher pitch
The perceived volume of a sound; determined by amplitude — larger amplitude = louder
Sound below 20 Hz — below the human hearing threshold; produced by earthquakes and large animals
Sound above 20,000 Hz — above the human hearing threshold; used in medical imaging and sonar
The reflection of a sound wave from a hard surface; used to calculate distances
Sound navigation and ranging — uses timed ultrasound pulses to measure distances underwater
Using reflected ultrasound pulses to build an image of internal structures (e.g. a foetus in the womb)
Waves produced by earthquakes that travel through the Earth
Longitudinal seismic waves that travel at different speeds through solids and liquids
Transverse seismic waves that cannot travel through a liquid
How much radiation energy arrives or is emitted per second, for each unit of area
An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it; it reflects and transmits none, and is the best possible emitter
A material that is always magnetic without needing an external field
A magnetic material that becomes temporarily magnetised inside a magnetic field
Materials that can be strongly magnetised: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel
Easy to magnetise and demagnetise — iron is the classic example
A region where a force acts on a magnetic material or current-carrying wire
